newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU negotiators to mull streamlined trade rules.
newsitem.headline: EU negotiators to mull streamlined trade rules.

text.p: A longtime issue facing the 15-country European Union is how to conduct external trade talks with one voice while trying to marry together the often contradictory positions of member states.

This has been most obvious in multilateral talks at the World Trade Organisation, where the EU's free traders are often at odds with their more protectionist partners over how far to open up sectors of the EU's single market to third countries.
Despite this, when the 15 countries have agreed, trade policy has been one of the EU's success stories.

The European Commission, the bloc's negotiator, says things would be easier if a new treaty to be agreed in Amsterdam next week were to give it powers to conduct WTO talks on trade in services and on intellectual property rights rules.
These new areas of trade were not covered by the old treaty, unlike trade in goods, meaning the Commission has to get a precise mandate from member states before taking part in talks.

The Commission describes the arrangement, along with the requirement that it report regularly to member states during talks and allow national officials to attend bilateral sessions with third country negotiators, as "unsustainable".

Going into the summit, however, member states are split three ways in their responses, with the Benelux countries, Finland and Sweden more or less in favour of giving the Commission the powers it wants.

France heads a group of the EU's southern countries who see the proposal as ceding ground to the bloc's trade liberals, a group Paris sees as championed by the chief negotiator himself, European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan, the British former Conservative minister.
Britain and Denmark, normally among the EU's trade liberals, are also uneasy, with their worries concerning what they see as a further loss of sovereignty to Brussels.
No one pretends the trade question will make or break the Amsterdam summit, with more than one diplomat describing it as one of the second-tier issues on the agenda.
However, in the long run, how the EU conducts itself in international dealings will become more pressing, particularly as more issues bubble up to the global level for negotiation.

Many see the most likely Amsterdam outcome as being no result, possibly after the Commission and the Dutch presidency have pulled their proposals to preserve the status quo in preference to any piecemeal extension of powers.
